lead: A four-stroke engine gives the piston four separate jobs — intake, compression, power, exhaust — and needs two crankshaft turns for one cycle. A two-stroke engine does the same gas exchange with ports in the cylinder wall and finishes one cycle in a single turn. The difference decides how often each cylinder fires, how smooth the torque is, how much fuel it uses and how it is cooled. You meet it in a Chennai scooter, a generator set and a truck engine.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for engine classification, and Chapter 1.2 for TDC, BDC and stroke.

blocks.text: A stroke is the piston's travel from top dead centre (TDC) to bottom dead centre (BDC), or the reverse. In a four-stroke engine each stroke is one direction of piston travel, which is half a crankshaft turn, or 180°CA (crank angle degrees). Four strokes take 4 × 180° = 720°CA, which is two full crankshaft revolutions.

Intake stroke: the piston moves from TDC to BDC with the inlet valve open. Falling cylinder pressure lets fresh fuel-air mixture (spark-ignition, SI, engine) or air (compression-ignition, CI, engine) enter. Compression stroke: both valves are closed and the piston moves from BDC to TDC, squeezing the charge and raising its pressure and temperature.

Power stroke: near TDC a spark ignites the mixture in an SI engine, or a fuel injector sprays diesel in a CI engine. Hot gas pushes the piston to BDC and the crankshaft delivers work. Exhaust stroke: the exhaust valve opens and the rising piston pushes burnt gas out of the cylinder.

Each cylinder gives one power stroke per 720°CA. The separate exhaust stroke gives clean gas exchange, which is why four-stroke engines dominate cars and trucks. Valve opening is not exactly at TDC or BDC; see Chapter 1.5 for lead, lag and overlap.

A two-stroke engine completes one cycle in one crankshaft revolution, 360°CA. It uses ports cut in the cylinder wall, opened and closed by the moving piston edge. A simple crankcase-scavenged engine has three sets of ports: intake (fresh charge into the crankcase), transfer (crankcase to cylinder) and exhaust (cylinder to atmosphere). The sealed crankcase acts as a pump.

Upward stroke: the piston rises from BDC. It first covers the transfer and exhaust ports, trapping the charge, then compresses it. At the same time the rising piston lowers the crankcase pressure, so fresh charge is drawn in through the intake port or a reed valve. The spark fires near TDC.

Downward stroke: the burning gas pushes the piston down, giving the power stroke. The exhaust port opens first and most burnt gas leaves. The transfer port opens next, and the compressed charge in the crankcase flows into the cylinder. This fresh charge sweeps the remaining burnt gas out; the process is called scavenging. The piston then covers the ports and compression begins again.

There is no separate intake or exhaust stroke. Scavenging arrangements include uniflow scavenging, where the fresh charge flows in one direction and an exhaust valve or port at the far end lets gas out, and loop scavenging, where the charge loops across the cylinder. Details are in Unit 4, Cooling, Lubrication and Supercharging. Port timing is drawn in Chapter 1.5.

The central difference is the number of power strokes per revolution. A four-stroke cylinder fires once every two revolutions; a two-stroke cylinder fires once every revolution. At the same speed and displacement, the two-stroke has twice as many power pulses in theory, and the torque is smoother because pulses arrive more often.

blocks.where: f₄ and f₂ are power strokes per second per cylinder; n is engine speed in rev/min. Cycle times are t₄ = 120/n s and t₂ = 60/n s.

blocks.text: Real engines do not get double power. Two-stroke scavenging is imperfect: some fresh charge escapes with the exhaust, so fuel consumption and unburnt hydrocarbon emissions are higher, and thermal efficiency is lower. A four-stroke engine's separate strokes fill and empty the cylinder better, giving lower fuel use and lower emissions. The cost is more parts: valves, camshaft, and a heavier cylinder head.

Cooling demand is higher in a two-stroke because it fires twice as often at the same speed. Small two-strokes use air cooling with fins; car four-strokes use liquid cooling. Two-strokes suit mopeds, chainsaws and outboard motors, where low weight and simple construction matter. Four-strokes suit cars, trucks and generator sets, where fuel economy and emissions matter.

A multi-stroke engine completes one cycle in k piston strokes, where k is greater than four. A six-stroke engine adds two strokes after exhaust: water is injected onto the hot cylinder to make steam, giving a second power stroke, and a final exhaust stroke clears the steam. The cycle angle is k × 180°CA; for six strokes it is 1080°CA, or three revolutions. The gain is recovery of exhaust heat. The cost is lower power per litre and extra hardware. More strokes per cycle mean fewer power strokes per revolution, so a multi-stroke engine is heavier and less powerful for its size unless heat recovery pays back. Other multi-stroke designs use extra strokes for better gas exchange. These engines remain in research and niche stationary use, not mass-produced cars.

figure.caption: One four-stroke cycle spans 720°CA with one power stroke; one two-stroke cycle spans 360°CA with one power stroke. The overlap near BDC is scavenging, where transfer and exhaust ports are both open.

spec.aria: A timeline compares the four-stroke cycle, with one power stroke in 720 crank degrees, and the two-stroke cycle, with one power stroke in 360 crank degrees.

examples.question: A four-stroke engine runs at 3000 rpm. Find the number of power strokes per second per cylinder and the time for one complete cycle. Repeat for a two-stroke engine at the same speed.
steps: Four-stroke: one cycle takes two revolutions, so cycle frequency = 50/2 = 25 cycles/s. Thus 25 power strokes/s per cylinder.
Four-stroke cycle time = 1/25 = 0.040 s. Equivalently, 2/50 = 0.040 s.
Two-stroke: one cycle takes one revolution, so cycle frequency = 50 cycles/s. Thus 50 power strokes/s per cylinder.
examples.answer: At 3000 rpm, the four-stroke cylinder gives 25 power strokes/s with a cycle time of 0.040 s; the two-stroke cylinder gives 50 power strokes/s with a cycle time of 0.020 s.
examples.check:
n_rpm = 3000
n_rps = n_rpm / 60
four = n_rps / 2
print(four)
print(1 / four)
print(n_rps)
print(1 / n_rps)

traps: Two-stroke does not mean two strokes per cycle in the four-stroke sense. It means one power stroke every revolution, with ports and scavenging; calling it 'two strokes' hides the gas exchange.
Do not double the power of a two-stroke blindly. Twice the power strokes is an ideal count; scavenging losses and lower trapping efficiency reduce real output.
Four-stroke cycle = 720°CA = 2 revolutions. Two-stroke cycle = 360°CA = 1 revolution. Mixing these gives wrong cycle time and wrong power-stroke frequency.
Scavenging is not supercharging. Scavenging pushes burnt gas out with fresh charge; supercharging raises the incoming charge density. Supercharging is in Unit 4.
Ports are not valves. In a piston-ported two-stroke the piston edge opens and closes the ports; there is no camshaft or poppet valve for those ports, though uniflow may use an exhaust valve.

quiz.q: How many crankshaft revolutions complete one cycle in a four-stroke engine and in a two-stroke engine?
Why can a two-stroke engine use piston-controlled ports instead of poppet valves?
quiz.a: The piston edge uncovers each port at the correct crank angle, so no camshaft or valve gear is needed for those ports. This reduces parts and cost.

quiz.q: A four-stroke four-cylinder engine runs at 1500 rpm. Find the total number of power strokes per second.
quiz.a: 1500 rpm = 25 rev/s. Per cylinder: 25/2 = 12.5 power strokes/s. For four cylinders: 12.5 × 4 = 50 power strokes/s.

quiz.q: A two-stroke single-cylinder engine runs at 6000 rpm. Find its cycle time and power strokes per second.
quiz.a: 6000 rpm = 100 rev/s. Cycle time = 1/100 = 0.010 s. Power strokes = 100 per second.

quiz.q: Why does a two-stroke engine usually emit more unburnt hydrocarbons than a four-stroke?
quiz.a: During scavenging the exhaust port and transfer port are open together. Some fresh fuel-air charge flows straight into the exhaust before the port closes, so unburnt fuel escapes. Short-circuiting is worse at light load.

quiz.q: Compare the cooling needs of four-stroke and two-stroke engines at the same speed.
quiz.a: A two-stroke fires twice as often per revolution, so it releases more heat per second for the same cylinder. It needs stronger cooling, often air cooling with fins in small sizes. A four-stroke fires half as often and can use liquid cooling in cars.

quiz.q: Name two scavenging arrangements used in two-stroke engines.
quiz.a: Uniflow scavenging and loop scavenging. Details are in Unit 4.

quiz.q: What is a transfer port and when does it open?
quiz.a: It is the passage from the crankcase to the cylinder. The piston uncovers it near BDC, after the exhaust port opens, so crankcase pressure pushes fresh charge into the cylinder and helps sweep out burnt gas.

beyond: Not for the exam. Two-stroke engines are returning in research as opposed-piston designs for hydrogen and high-efficiency range extenders, because they are compact and have few parts. Multi-stroke concepts are studied for waste-heat recovery, using steam or extra expansion strokes. Search for 'opposed-piston two-stroke', 'six-stroke engine' and 'scavenging efficiency' if you want the next layer. Emission rules, not thermodynamics, decide which of these reaches the road.
